catalog_quote: d. When two or more vowels follow each other, each is pronounced separately and the transition between them is soft; the symbol, <between two vowels> indicates that the second has a separate onset. e. The diphthongs ai or ei, as in sampai, sampei, and au as in pulau do not occur <in the language>. ... h. Syllables which are underlined carry the stress. i. The e and i, which occur frequently as suffixes, are pronounced very clearly. ... k. This language is, in its pure form, spoken only in Rumakai and in part of the Kairatoe district (Seram). However, it is understood well by the original inhabitants of the island of Haruku, and partly by the inhabitants of Saparua and Nusalaut.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The source states no rule; it marks the stressed syllable of every entry by underlining. Reading the underlining on pp. 90-93 (c. 300 items), the stressed syllable is the penultimate one in essentially every polysyllabic word, including Malay loans (my transcription of the underlining with an acute: Pátan, Oéroe, Oéwa, Pólon, Tarína, Talapési, Hiroe kamátai, Ai manteroéni, Panikoe-níkoe, Malóna, Mahína, Kapítan, Agáma, Sembáhjang, Roémah, Malápat). In phrases each word carries its own penultimate stress (Reoe malóna ma'amína'e). So: fixed penultimate word stress, inferred from marked data, not from a stated rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. A handful of underlinings on pp. 90-91 are hard to read (e.g. 'Hoetoewa oekoe', 'Oerata'); no systematic non-penultimate class is visible.
new_statements.domain_note: Citation-form wordlist entries and short phrases collected in 1895 by a native-school teacher for the Holle questionnaire; the stress placement is a reader's inference from the underlining, not a statement by the source. The list is for the Rumakai (Rumahkay) variety, treated as a dialect of Kamarian by Collins 1983:118-119 and Grimes & Edwards 2026:383; Ethnologue lists no dialects for kzx.
new_statements.identity_note: The only first-hand stress data are for the Rumakai (Rumahkay) village variety (Holle list 27, 1895). Collins 1983:118-119 calls Rumakai 'a dialect of Kamarian' and Grimes & Edwards 2026:383 list Rumakai and Tihulale as 'other varieties of Kamarian'; Taguchi 1989 (WILC 6) groups Kamarian, Rumahkay, Seruawan and Tihulale together under his 'KAIBOBO' language. Glottolog has no separate code for Rumakai; it falls under kama1362. Kamarian itself is dormant (Ethnologue: no known L1 speakers; c. 3 in 1985).

sources.note: Collector's explanatory note h (p. 89): 'Syllables which are underlined carry the stress.' The printed list keeps the underlining; across c. 300 items on pp. 90-93 (including Malay loans such as Kapitan, Agama, Sembahjang, Roemah) the underlined syllable is the penultimate one in essentially every polysyllabic word. No rule is stated; penultimate placement is the reader's inference from the marked forms. Rumakai is a dialect of Kamarian per Collins 1983:118-119 and Grimes & Edwards 2026:383.

sources.citation: Grimes, Charles E. & Owen Edwards. 2026. The Austronesian languages of eastern Indonesia and Timor-Leste. Berlin: Language Science Press (Studies in Diversity Linguistics 526).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Uses Kamarian data (van Ekris 1864, Holle); p. 383: 'the variety of Kamarian from the village of the same name has **l > r before or after e. Other varieties of Kamarian (Tihulale, and Rumakai) have **l > l adjacent to e.' Only a general remark p. 114 'penultimate stress is the normal rule for Wallacean languages'; no Kamarian-specific stress statement.

sources.citation: Collins, James T. 1983. The historical relationships of the languages of Central Maluku, Indonesia. Pacific Linguistics D-47. Canberra: ANU.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Comparative study; Kamarian used as data throughout, 'Rumakai (a dialect of Kamarian)' p. 118-119. Stress statements only for other branches: p. 82 'Stress in Hoamoal languages is always penultimate; if a suffix or particle is added to the word the stress shifts accordingly. In Asilulu this is not the case. The stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root word; additions of suffixes do not affect this stress.' Silent on Kamarian stress.
